title: Element 7: Chemical and Biological Agents
learningObjectives: Classify hazardous substances by their health effects and routes of entry
Explain the principles of occupational exposure limits (OELs)
Describe the COSHH assessment process and hierarchy of controls
Identify key biological hazards and appropriate control measures

content.text: Hazardous substances can enter the body through four routes. Understanding the route of entry determines which controls are most effective.

rows: Breathing in gases, vapours, dusts, fumes, mists
H2S, silica dust, welding fume, spray paint vapour
Substance passes through the skin or eyes
Swallowing contaminated food, drink, or hand-to-mouth transfer
No eating/drinking in work areas, handwashing
Substance injected through a puncture wound
High-pressure hydraulic fluid injection, needle-stick injuries
Safe needle handling, pressure system maintenance

content.text: Inhalation is the most common and most dangerous route of entry in industrial workplaces. Always prioritise controls that prevent substances from becoming airborne before relying on RPE.

rows: Immediate effects from short-term high-dose exposure
H2S poisoning, acid burns, solvent narcosis
Long-term effects from repeated low-dose exposure over years
Effect at site distant from entry point
Lead affecting the nervous system after inhalation/ingestion
Causes allergic reaction (worsens with each exposure)
Isocyanates (spray painting), latex, flour dust — occupational asthma

content.term: Workplace Exposure Limit (WEL) / Occupational Exposure Limit (OEL)
content.text: The maximum concentration of a substance in workplace air to which workers may be exposed. Set to protect workers' health. Two types: Time-Weighted Average (TWA — 8-hour average) and Short-Term Exposure Limit (STEL — 15-minute average).

rows: Fatal at 300+ ppm; olfactory fatigue at 100+ ppm

content.text: H2S is present in sour crude oil, sour gas, and wastewater in Gulf O&G operations. Workers must wear personal H2S gas detectors set to alarm at 5 ppm (low alarm) and 10 ppm (high alarm). Areas where H2S concentrations could exceed the IDLH (Immediately Dangerous to Life or Health — 100 ppm) require SCBA. Understanding H2S response procedures is MANDATORY knowledge for any Gulf HSE professional.
7.4 COSHH Assessment — Control of Substances Hazardous to Health
COSHH (UK framework) or equivalent hazardous substance assessment requires eight steps. The principles are internationally applicable:

items: 1. Assess the risk — Identify substances, routes of exposure, who is at risk, how often and for how long
2. Decide what controls are needed — Apply the hierarchy of controls
3. Prevent or adequately control exposure — Implement controls
4. Ensure controls are used and maintained — Inspect, test, and maintain controls
5. Monitor exposure — Measure workplace air concentrations against OELs
6. Carry out health surveillance — Medical monitoring for workers at significant risk
7. Prepare emergency plans — Spill response, first aid for chemical exposure
8. Ensure workers are properly informed and trained

content.text: 7.5 Hierarchy of Controls for Chemical Hazards

items: Elimination — Remove the substance entirely (reformulate product, change process)
Substitution — Replace with a less hazardous substance (e.g., water-based instead of solvent-based paint)
Enclosure — Fully enclose the process so substance cannot escape
Local Exhaust Ventilation (LEV) — Extract substance at source before it spreads into room air
General Ventilation — Dilute contaminant with clean air (less effective; used for low-toxicity substances)
Reduction of exposure time — Limit how long any individual is exposed
RPE — Respiratory protective equipment as last resort (must be correctly selected, fitted, and worn)

rows: Water temperature control (>60°C), closed systems, vaccination
Sewer workers, outdoor workers near water
Healthcare workers, camel farm workers in Arabian Peninsula

content.text: MERS-CoV (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome) has been found in camels and can be transmitted to humans. In Gulf countries, this is a specific biological hazard that HSE professionals should be aware of, particularly in agricultural and veterinary settings. Additionally, wastewater treatment in the Gulf presents Legionella risk in cooling towers — regular water quality testing and disinfection are required.
